title: Pathology Detection and Scan Triage

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Pathology detection and scan triage covers software that reads medical images to find signs of disease and software that decides which studies a radiologist should read first. Detection work spans chest radiographs, mammograms, CT of the head and chest, and MRI, and it usually flags a finding rather than issuing a diagnosis. Triage work sorts an existing worklist, moving studies that look urgent to the top so a reader sees them sooner. The two functions are often sold together, but they carry different risks and are regulated differently.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on the imaging pipeline a hospital already has: the picture archiving and communication system, the radiology information system, and the modality worklist. A model is usually packaged as a container or service that receives images over standards such as DICOM and HL7 and returns a result to the viewer or the worklist. Some products run on servers inside the hospital, and some run in a vendor cloud, which raises questions about where patient images are stored and who can reach them. Compute ranges from a single GPU appliance to shared cluster capacity, and the site tracks 1000 medical AI models across this and other clinical areas.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Most of these tools are trained on large sets of images that have been labeled by radiologists, either with a diagnosis, a bounding box around a finding, or a report sentence. Convolutional networks and, more recently, vision transformers are the common architectures, and training is judged against held out data using measures such as sensitivity, specificity, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Triage tools are evaluated differently, often by how much they shorten the time to a report for urgent cases rather than by accuracy alone. Deployment adds a monitoring layer, because image quality, scanner vendor, and patient mix at a new site can shift performance away from what was measured in the training study.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: In the United States, most of these products reach the market through the FDA clearance pathways for software as a medical device, and in Europe they need a CE mark under the medical device rules. Clearance is tied to a stated intended use, a population, and often a specific scanner or protocol, so using the tool outside those bounds is a change in practice that a quality team should record. Liability is live: the site tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, and the site also holds 229 compliance and regulation pages. Provenance matters in both directions, meaning which model version produced a flag and which images and labels trained it, because a radiologist who overrides a flag needs to know what was overridden.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The near term is less about new architectures and more about fitting these tools into reading workflow without adding alerts that readers learn to ignore. Expect more work on prospective monitoring, on detecting when a model drifts at a new site, and on reporting standards that make a model's output legible in the patient record. Triage is likely to spread from stroke and intracranial hemorrhage into more routine queues, where the benefit is throughput rather than emergency speed. Regulation will keep tightening around post market surveillance and labeling, and the open question is how liability is shared when a cleared tool misses a finding that a human reader would also have missed.
